1 --- 2 name: visual-explainer 3 description: Generate beautiful, self-contained HTML pages that visually explain systems, code changes, plans, and data. Use when the user asks for a diagram, architecture overview, diff review, plan review, project recap, comparison table, or any visual explanation of technical concepts. Also use proactively when you are about to render a complex ASCII table (4+ rows or 3+ columns) — present it as a styled HTML page instead. 4 license: MIT 5 compatibility: Requires a browser to view generated HTML files. Optional surf-cli for AI image generation. 6 metadata: 7 author: nicobailon 8 version: "0.6.3" 9 --- 10 11 # Visual Explainer 12 13 Generate self-contained HTML files for technical diagrams, visualizations, and data tables. Always open the result in the browser. Never fall back to ASCII art when this skill is loaded. 14 15 **Proactive table rendering.** When you're about to present tabular data as an ASCII box-drawing table in the terminal (comparisons, audits, feature matrices, status reports, any structured rows/columns), generate an HTML page instead. The threshold: if the table has 4+ rows or 3+ columns, it belongs in the browser. Don't wait for the user to ask — render it as HTML automatically and tell them the file path. You can still include a brief text summary in the chat, but the table itself should be the HTML page. 16 17 ## Available Commands 18 19 Detailed prompt templates in `./commands/`. In Pi, these are slash commands (`/diff-review`). In Claude Code, namespaced (`/visual-explainer:diff-review`). In Codex, use `/prompts:diff-review` (if installed to `~/.codex/prompts/`) or invoke `$visual-explainer` and describe the workflow. 20 21 | Command | What it does | 22 |---------|-------------| 23 | `generate-web-diagram` | Generate an HTML diagram for any topic | 24 | `generate-visual-plan` | Generate a visual implementation plan for a feature | 25 | `generate-slides` | Generate a magazine-quality slide deck | 26 | `diff-review` | Visual diff review with architecture comparison and code review | 27 | `plan-review` | Compare a plan against the codebase with risk assessment | 28 | `project-recap` | Mental model snapshot for context-switching back to a project | 29 | `fact-check` | Verify accuracy of a document against actual code | 30 | `share` | Deploy an HTML page to Vercel and get a live URL | 31 32 ## Workflow 33 34 ### 1. Think (5 seconds, not 5 minutes) 35 36 Before writing HTML, commit to a direction. Don't default to "dark theme with blue accents" every time. 37 38 **Visual is always default.** Even essays, blog posts, and articles get visual treatment — extract structure into cards, diagrams, grids, tables. 39 40 Prose patterns (lead paragraphs, pull quotes, callout boxes) are **accent elements** within visual pages, not a separate mode. Use them to highlight key points or provide breathing room, but the page structure remains visual. 41 42 For prose accents, see "Prose Page Elements" in `./references/css-patterns.md`. For everything else, use the standard freeform approach with aesthetic directions below. 43 44 **Who is looking?** A developer understanding a system? A PM seeing the big picture? A team reviewing a proposal? This shapes information density and visual complexity. 45 46 **What type of content?** Architecture, flowchart, sequence, data flow, schema/ER, state machine, mind map, class diagram, C4 architecture, data table, timeline, dashboard, or prose-first page. Each has distinct layout needs and rendering approaches (see Diagram Types below). 47 48 **What aesthetic?** Pick one and commit. The constrained aesthetics (Blueprint, Editorial, Paper/ink) are safer — they have specific requirements that prevent generic output. The flexible ones (IDE-inspired) require more discipline. 49 50 **Constrained aesthetics (prefer these):** 51 - Blueprint (technical drawing feel, subtle grid background, deep slate/blue palette, monospace labels, precise borders) — see `websocket-implementation-plan.html` for reference 52 - Editorial (serif headlines like Instrument Serif or Crimson Pro, generous whitespace, muted earth tones or deep navy + gold) 53 - Paper/ink (warm cream `#faf7f5` background, terracotta/sage accents, informal feel) 54 - Monochrome terminal (green/amber on near-black, monospace everything, CRT glow optional) 55 56 **Flexible aesthetics (use with caution):** 57 - IDE-inspired (borrow a real, named color scheme: Dracula, Nord, Catppuccin Mocha/Latte, Solarized Dark/Light, Gruvbox, One Dark, Rosé Pine) — commit to the actual palette, don't approximate 58 - Data-dense (small type, tight spacing, maximum information, muted colors) 59 60 **Explicitly forbidden:** 61 - Neon dashboard (cyan + magenta + purple on dark) — always produces AI slop 62 - Gradient mesh (pink/purple/cyan blobs) — too generic 63 - Any combination of Inter font + violet/indigo accents + gradient text 64 65 Vary the choice each time. If the last diagram was dark and technical, make the next one light and editorial. The swap test: if you replaced your styling with a generic dark theme and nobody would notice the difference, you haven't designed anything. 66 67 ### 2. Structure 68 69 **Read the reference material** before generating. Don't memorize it — read it each time to absorb the patterns. 70 - For text-heavy architecture overviews (card content matters more than topology): read `./templates/architecture.html` 71 - For flowcharts, sequence diagrams, ER, state machines, mind maps, class diagrams, C4: read `./templates/mermaid-flowchart.html` 72 - For data tables, comparisons, audits, feature matrices: read `./templates/data-table.html` 73 - For slide deck presentations (when `--slides` flag is present or `/generate-slides` is invoked): read `./templates/slide-deck.html` and `./references/slide-patterns.md` 74 - For prose-heavy publishable pages (READMEs, articles, blog posts, essays): read the "Prose Page Elements" section in `./references/css-patterns.md` and "Typography by Content Voice" in `./references/libraries.md` 75 76 **For CSS/layout patterns and SVG connectors**, read `./references/css-patterns.md`. 77 78 **For pages with 4+ sections** (reviews, recaps, dashboards), also read `./references/responsive-nav.md` for section navigation with sticky sidebar TOC on desktop and horizontal scrollable bar on mobile. 79 80 **Choosing a rendering approach:** 81 82 | Content type | Approach | Why | 83 |---|---|---| 84 | Architecture (text-heavy) | CSS Grid cards + flow arrows | Rich card content (descriptions, code, tool lists) needs CSS control | 85 | Architecture (topology-focused) | **Mermaid** | Visible connections between components need automatic edge routing | 86 | Flowchart / pipeline | **Mermaid** | Automatic node positioning and edge routing | 87 | Sequence diagram | **Mermaid** | Lifelines, messages, and activation boxes need automatic layout | 88 | Data flow | **Mermaid** with edge labels | Connections and data descriptions need automatic edge routing | 89 | ER / schema diagram | **Mermaid** | Relationship lines between many entities need auto-routing | 90 | State machine | **Mermaid** | State transitions with labeled edges need automatic layout | 91 | Mind map | **Mermaid** | Hierarchical branching needs automatic positioning | 92 | Class diagram | **Mermaid** | Inheritance, composition, aggregation lines with automatic routing | 93 | C4 architecture | **Mermaid** | Use `graph TD` + `subgraph` for C4 (not native `C4Context` — it ignores themes) | 94 | Data table | HTML `` | Semantic markup, accessibility, copy-paste behavior | 95 | Timeline | CSS (central line + cards) | Simple linear layout doesn't need a layout engine | 96 | Dashboard | CSS Grid + Chart.js | Card grid with embedded charts | 97 98 **Mermaid theming:** Always use `theme: 'base'` with custom `themeVariables` so colors match your page palette. Use `layout: 'elk'` for complex graphs (requires the `@mermaid-js/layout-elk` package — see `./references/libraries.md` for the CDN import). Override Mermaid's SVG classes with CSS for pixel-perfect control. See `./references/libraries.md` for full theming guide. 99 100 **Mermaid containers:** Always center Mermaid diagrams with `display: flex; justify-content: center;`. Add zoom controls (+/−/reset/expand) to every `.mermaid-wrap` container. Include the click-to-expand JavaScript so clicking the diagram (or the ⛶ button) opens it full-size in a new tab. 101 102 **⚠️ Never use bare `
`.** It renders but has no zoom/pan controls — diagrams become tiny and unusable. Always use the full `diagram-shell` pattern from `templates/mermaid-flowchart.html`: the HTML structure (`.diagram-shell` > `.mermaid-wrap` > `.zoom-controls` + `.mermaid-viewport` > `.mermaid-canvas`), the CSS, and the ~200-line JS module for zoom/pan/fit. Copy it wholesale.
   103	
   104	**Mermaid scaling:** Diagrams with 10+ nodes render too small by default. For 10-12 nodes, increase `fontSize` in themeVariables to 18-20px and set `INITIAL_ZOOM` to 1.5-1.6. For 15+ elements, don't try to scale — use the hybrid pattern instead (simple Mermaid overview + CSS Grid cards). See "Architecture / System Diagrams" below.
   105	
   106	**Mermaid layout direction:** Prefer `flowchart TD` (top-down) over `flowchart LR` (left-to-right) for complex diagrams. LR spreads horizontally and makes labels unreadable when there are many nodes. Use LR only for simple 3-4 node linear flows. See `./references/libraries.md` "Layout Direction: TD vs LR".
   107	
   108	**Mermaid line breaks in flowchart labels:** Use `
` inside quoted labels. Never use escaped newlines like `\n` (Mermaid renders them as literal text in HTML output). Example: `A["Copilot Backend
/api + /api/voicebot"]`.
   109	
   110	**Mermaid CSS class collision constraint:** Never define `.node` as a page-level CSS class. Mermaid.js uses `.node` internally on SVG `` elements with `transform: translate(x, y)` for positioning. Page-level `.node` styles (hover transforms, box-shadows) leak into diagrams and break layout. Use the namespaced `.ve-card` class for card components instead. The only safe way to style Mermaid's `.node` is scoped under `.mermaid` (e.g., `.mermaid .node rect`).
   111	
   112	**AI-generated illustrations (optional).** If [surf-cli](https://github.com/nicobailon/surf-cli) is available, you can generate images via Gemini and embed them in the page for creative, illustrative, explanatory, educational, or decorative purposes. Check availability with `which surf`. If available:
   113	
   114	```bash
   115	# Generate to a temp file (use --aspect-ratio for control)
   116	surf gemini "descriptive prompt" --generate-image /tmp/ve-img.png --aspect-ratio 16:9
   117	
   118	# Base64 encode for self-containment (macOS)
   119	IMG=$(base64 -i /tmp/ve-img.png)
   120	# Linux: IMG=$(base64 -w 0 /tmp/ve-img.png)
   121	
   122	# Embed in HTML and clean up
   123	# 
   124	rm /tmp/ve-img.png
   125	```
   126	
   127	See `./references/css-patterns.md` for image container styles (hero banners, inline illustrations, captions).
   128	
   129	**When to use:** Hero banners that establish the page's visual tone. Conceptual illustrations for abstract systems that Mermaid can't express (physical infrastructure, user journeys, mental models). Educational diagrams that benefit from artistic or photorealistic rendering. Decorative accents that reinforce the aesthetic.
   130	
   131	**When to skip:** Anything Mermaid or CSS handles well. Generic decoration that doesn't convey meaning. Data-heavy pages where images would distract. Always degrade gracefully — if surf isn't available, skip images without erroring. The page should stand on its own with CSS and typography alone.
   132	
   133	**Prompt craft:** Match the image to the page's palette and aesthetic direction. Specify the style (3D render, technical illustration, watercolor, isometric, flat vector, etc.) and mention dominant colors from your CSS variables. Use `--aspect-ratio 16:9` for hero banners, `--aspect-ratio 1:1` for inline illustrations. Keep prompts specific — "isometric illustration of a message queue with cyan nodes on dark navy background" beats "a diagram of a queue."
   134	
   135	### 3. Style
   136	
   137	Apply these principles to every diagram:
   138	
   139	**Typography is the diagram.** Pick a distinctive font pairing from the list in `./references/libraries.md`. Every page should use a different pairing from recent generations.
   140	
   141	**Forbidden as `--font-body`:** Inter, Roboto, Arial, Helvetica, system-ui alone. These are AI slop signals.
   142	
   143	**Good pairings (use these):**
   144	- DM Sans + Fira Code (technical, precise)
   145	- Instrument Serif + JetBrains Mono (editorial, refined)
   146	- IBM Plex Sans + IBM Plex Mono (reliable, readable)
   147	- Bricolage Grotesque + Fragment Mono (bold, characterful)
   148	- Plus Jakarta Sans + Azeret Mono (rounded, approachable)
   149	
   150	Load via `` in ``. Include a system font fallback in the `font-family` stack for offline resilience.
   151	
   152	**Color tells a story.** Use CSS custom properties for the full palette. Define at minimum: `--bg`, `--surface`, `--border`, `--text`, `--text-dim`, and 3-5 accent colors. Each accent should have a full and a dim variant (for backgrounds). Name variables semantically when possible (`--pipeline-step` not `--blue-3`). Support both themes.
   153	
   154	**Forbidden accent colors:** `#8b5cf6` `#7c3aed` `#a78bfa` (indigo/violet), `#d946ef` (fuchsia), the cyan-magenta-pink combination. These are Tailwind defaults that signal zero design intent.
   155	
   156	**Good accent palettes (use these):**
   157	- Terracotta + sage (`#c2410c`, `#65a30d`) — warm, earthy
   158	- Teal + slate (`#0891b2`, `#0369a1`) — technical, precise
   159	- Rose + cranberry (`#be123c`, `#881337`) — editorial, refined
   160	- Amber + emerald (`#d97706`, `#059669`) — data-focused
   161	- Deep blue + gold (`#1e3a5f`, `#d4a73a`) — premium, sophisticated
   162	
   163	Put your primary aesthetic in `:root` and the alternate in the media query:
   164	
   165	```css
   166	/* Light-first (editorial, paper/ink, blueprint): */
   167	:root { /* light values */ }
   168	@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root { /* dark values */ } }
   169	
   170	/* Dark-first (neon, IDE-inspired, terminal): */
   171	:root { /* dark values */ }
   172	@media (prefers-color-scheme: light) { :root { /* light values */ } }
   173	```
   174	
   175	**Surfaces whisper, they don't shout.** Build depth through subtle lightness shifts (2-4% between levels), not dramatic color changes. Borders should be low-opacity rgba (`rgba(255,255,255,0.08)` in dark mode, `rgba(0,0,0,0.08)` in light) — visible when you look, invisible when you don't.
   176	
   177	**Backgrounds create atmosphere.** Don't use flat solid colors for the page background. Subtle gradients, faint grid patterns via CSS, or gentle radial glows behind focal areas. The background should feel like a space, not a void.
   178	
   179	**Visual weight signals importance.** Not every section deserves equal visual treatment. Executive summaries and key metrics should dominate the viewport on load (larger type, more padding, subtle accent-tinted background zone). Reference sections (file maps, dependency lists, decision logs) should be compact and stay out of the way. Use `
/` for sections that are useful but not primary — the collapsible pattern is in `./references/css-patterns.md`.
   180	
   181	**Surface depth creates hierarchy.** Vary card depth to signal what matters. Hero sections get elevated shadows and accent-tinted backgrounds (`ve-card--hero` pattern). Body content stays flat (default `.ve-card`). Code blocks and secondary content feel recessed (`ve-card--recessed`). See the depth tiers in `./references/css-patterns.md`. Don't make everything elevated — when everything pops, nothing does.
   182	
   183	**Animation earns its place.** Staggered fade-ins on page load are almost always worth it — they guide the eye through the diagram's hierarchy. Mix animation types by role: `fadeUp` for cards, `fadeScale` for KPIs and badges, `drawIn` for SVG connectors, `countUp` for hero numbers. Hover transitions on interactive-feeling elements make the diagram feel alive. Always respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. CSS transitions and keyframes handle most cases. For orchestrated multi-element sequences, anime.js via CDN is available (see `./references/libraries.md`).
   184	
   185	**Forbidden animations:**
   186	- Animated glowing box-shadows (`@keyframes glow { box-shadow: 0 0 20px... }`) — this is AI slop
   187	- Pulsing/breathing effects on static content
   188	- Continuous animations that run after page load (except for progress indicators)
   189	
   190	Keep animations purposeful: entrance reveals, hover feedback, and user-initiated interactions. Nothing should glow or pulse on its own.
   191	
   192	### 4. Deliver
   193	
   194	**Output location:** Write to `~/.agent/diagrams/`. Use a descriptive filename based on content: `modem-architecture.html`, `pipeline-flow.html`, `schema-overview.html`. The directory persists across sessions.
   195	
   196	**Open in browser:**
   197	- macOS: `open ~/.agent/diagrams/filename.html`
   198	- Linux: `xdg-open ~/.agent/diagrams/filename.html`
   199	
   200	**Tell the user** the file path so they can re-open or share it.
   201	
   202	## Diagram Types
   203	
   204	### Architecture / System Diagrams
   205	Three approaches depending on complexity:
   206	
   207	**Simple topology (under 10 elements):** Use Mermaid. A `graph TD` with custom `themeVariables` produces readable diagrams with automatic edge routing.
   208	
   209	**Text-heavy overviews (under 15 elements):** CSS Grid with explicit row/column placement. Sections as rounded cards with colored borders and monospace labels. Vertical flow arrows between sections. The reference template at `./templates/architecture.html` demonstrates this pattern. Use when cards need descriptions, code references, tool lists, or other rich content that Mermaid nodes can't hold.
   210	
   211	**Complex architectures (15+ elements):** Use the **hybrid pattern** — a simple Mermaid overview (5-8 nodes showing module relationships) followed by detailed CSS Grid cards for each module's internals. This gives you visual topology AND readable details. The overview diagram uses module names with `` tags for key function names. The cards below show full function lists with new/modified badges. Never try to cram 15+ elements into a single Mermaid diagram — it will render unreadably small even with zoom controls.
   212	
   213	### Flowcharts / Pipelines
   214	**Use Mermaid.** Automatic node positioning and edge routing produces proper diagrams with connecting lines, decision diamonds, and parallel branches — dramatically better than CSS flexbox with arrow characters. Prefer `graph TD` (top-down); use `graph LR` only for simple 3-4 node linear flows. Color-code node types with Mermaid's `classDef` or rely on `themeVariables` for automatic styling.
   215	
   216	### Sequence Diagrams
   217	**Use Mermaid.** Lifelines, messages, activation boxes, notes, and loops all need automatic layout. Use Mermaid's `sequenceDiagram` syntax. Style actors and messages via CSS overrides on `.actor`, `.messageText`, `.activation` classes.
   218	
   219	### Data Flow Diagrams
   220	**Use Mermaid.** Data flow diagrams emphasize connections over boxes — exactly what Mermaid excels at. Use `graph TD` (or `graph LR` for simple linear flows) with edge labels for data descriptions. Thicker, colored edges for primary flows. Source/sink nodes styled differently from transform nodes via Mermaid's `classDef`.
   221	
   222	### Schema / ER Diagrams
   223	**Use Mermaid.** Relationship lines between entities need automatic routing. Use Mermaid's `erDiagram` syntax with entity attributes. Style via `themeVariables` and CSS overrides on `.er.entityBox` and `.er.relationshipLine`.
   224	
   225	### State Machines / Decision Trees
   226	**Use Mermaid.** Use `stateDiagram-v2` for states with labeled transitions. Supports nested states, forks, joins, and notes. Decision trees can use `graph TD` with diamond decision nodes.
   227	
   228	**`stateDiagram-v2` label caveat:** Transition labels have a strict parser — colons, parentheses, `
`, HTML entities, and most special characters cause silent parse failures ("Syntax error in text"). If your labels need any of these (e.g., `cancel()`, `curate: true`, multi-line labels), use `flowchart TD` instead with rounded nodes and quoted edge labels (`|"label text"|`). Flowcharts handle all special characters and support `
` for line breaks. Reserve `stateDiagram-v2` for simple single-word or plain-text labels.
   229	
   230	### Mind Maps / Hierarchical Breakdowns
   231	**Use Mermaid.** Use `mindmap` syntax for hierarchical branching from a root node. Mermaid handles the radial layout automatically. Style with `themeVariables` to control node colors at each depth level.
   232	
   233	### Class Diagrams
   234	**Use Mermaid.** Use `classDiagram` syntax for domain modeling, OOP design, and entity relationships with typed properties and methods. Supports relationships: association (`-->`), composition (`*--`), aggregation (`o--`), and inheritance (`<|--`). Add multiplicity labels (e.g., `"1" --> "*"`) and abstract/interface markers (`<>`, `<>`). For simple entity boxes without OOP semantics (no methods, no inheritance), prefer `erDiagram` instead — it produces cleaner output for pure data modeling.
   235	
   236	### C4 Architecture Diagrams
   237	**Use Mermaid flowchart syntax — NOT native C4.** Use `graph TD` with `subgraph` blocks for C4 boundaries. Native `C4Context` hardcodes sharp corners, its own font, blue icons, and inline SVG colors that ignore `themeVariables` — it always clashes with custom palettes.
   238	
   239	**Flowchart-as-C4 pattern:** Persons → rounded nodes `(("Name"))`, systems → rectangles `["Name"]`, databases → cylinders `[("Name")]`, boundaries → `subgraph` blocks, relationships → labeled arrows `-->|"protocol"|`. Use `classDef` + `:::className` to visually differentiate external systems (e.g., dashed borders). This inherits `themeVariables`, `fontFamily`, and CSS overrides like every other Mermaid diagram.
   240	
   241	### Data Tables / Comparisons / Audits
   242	Use a real `
` element — not CSS Grid pretending to be a table. Tables get accessibility, copy-paste behavior, and column alignment for free. The reference template at `./templates/data-table.html` demonstrates all patterns below. 243 244 **Use proactively.** Any time you'd render an ASCII box-drawing table in the terminal, generate an HTML table instead. This includes: requirement audits (request vs plan), feature comparisons, status reports, configuration matrices, test result summaries, dependency lists, permission tables, API endpoint inventories — any structured rows and columns. 245 246 Layout patterns: 247 - Sticky `` so headers stay visible when scrolling long tables 248 - Alternating row backgrounds via `tr:nth-child(even)` (subtle, 2-3% lightness shift) 249 - First column optionally sticky for wide tables with horizontal scroll 250 - Responsive wrapper with `overflow-x: auto` for tables wider than the viewport 251 - Column width hints via `` or `th` widths — let text-heavy columns breathe 252 - Row hover highlight for scanability 253 254 Status indicators (use styled `` elements, never emoji): 255 - Match/pass/yes: colored dot or checkmark with green background 256 - Gap/fail/no: colored dot or cross with red background 257 - Partial/warning: amber indicator 258 - Neutral/info: dim text or muted badge 259 260 Cell content: 261 - Wrap long text naturally — don't truncate or force single-line 262 - Use `` for technical references within cells 263 - Secondary detail text in `` with dimmed color 264 - Keep numeric columns right-aligned with `tabular-nums` 265 266 ### Timeline / Roadmap Views 267 Vertical or horizontal timeline with a central line (CSS pseudo-element). Phase markers as circles on the line. Content cards branching left/right (alternating) or all to one side. Date labels on the line. Color progression from past (muted) to future (vivid). 268 269 ### Dashboard / Metrics Overview 270 Card grid layout. Hero numbers large and prominent. Sparklines via inline SVG ``. Progress bars via CSS `linear-gradient` on a div. For real charts (bar, line, pie), use **Chart.js via CDN** (see `./references/libraries.md`). KPI cards with trend indicators (up/down arrows, percentage deltas). 271 272 ### Implementation Plans 273 274 For visualizing implementation plans, extension designs, or feature specifications. The goal is **understanding the approach**, not reading the full source code. 275 276 **Don't dump full files.** Displaying entire source files inline overwhelms the page and defeats the purpose of a visual explanation. Instead: 277 - Show **file structure with descriptions** — list functions/exports with one-line explanations 278 - Show **key snippets only** — the 5-10 lines that illustrate the core logic 279 - Use **collapsible sections** for full code if truly needed 280 281 **Code blocks require explicit formatting.** Without `white-space: pre-wrap`, code runs together into an unreadable wall. See the "Code Blocks" section in `./references/css-patterns.md` for the correct pattern. 282 283 **Structure for implementation plans:** 284 1. Overview/purpose (what problem does this solve?) 285 2. Flow diagram (Mermaid or CSS cards) 286 3. File structure with descriptions (not full code) 287 4. Key implementation details (snippets) 288 5. API/interface summary 289 6. Usage examples 290 291 ### Documentation (READMEs, Library Docs, API References) 292 293 When visualizing documentation, extract structure into visual elements: 294 295 | Content | Visual Treatment | 296 |---------|------------------| 297 | Features | Card grid (2-3 columns) | 298 | Install/setup steps | Numbered cards or vertical flow | 299 | API endpoints/commands | Table with sticky header | 300 | Config options | Table | 301 | Architecture | Mermaid diagram or CSS card layout | 302 | Comparisons | Side-by-side panels or table | 303 | Warnings/notes | Callout boxes | 304 305 Don't just format the prose — transform it. A feature list becomes a card grid. Install steps become a numbered flow. An API reference becomes a table. 306 307 ### Prose Accent Elements 308 309 Use these sparingly within visual pages to highlight key points or provide breathing room. See "Prose Page Elements" in `./references/css-patterns.md` for CSS patterns. 310 311 - **Lead paragraph** — larger intro text to set context before diving into cards/grids 312 - **Pull quote** — highlight a key insight; one per page maximum 313 - **Callout box** — warnings, tips, important notes 314 - **Section divider** — visual break between major sections 315 316 **When to use:** A visual page explaining an essay might use a lead paragraph for the thesis, then cards for key arguments. A README visualization might use callout boxes for warnings but otherwise stay card/table-focused. 317 318 ## Slide Deck Mode 319 320 An alternative output format for presenting content as a magazine-quality slide presentation instead of a scrollable page. **Opt-in only** — the agent generates slides when the user invokes `/generate-slides`, passes `--slides` to an existing prompt (e.g., `/diff-review --slides`), or explicitly asks for a slide deck. Never auto-select slide format. 321 322 **Before generating slides**, read `./references/slide-patterns.md` (engine CSS, slide types, transitions, nav chrome, presets) and `./templates/slide-deck.html` (reference template showing all 10 types). Also read `./references/css-patterns.md` for shared patterns and `./references/libraries.md` for Mermaid/Chart.js theming. 323 324 **Slides are not pages reformatted.** They're a different medium. Each slide is exactly one viewport tall (100dvh) with no scrolling. Typography is 2–3× larger. Compositions are bolder. The agent composes a narrative arc (impact → context → deep dive → resolution) rather than mechanically paginating the source. 325 326 **Content completeness.** Changing the medium does not mean dropping content. Follow the "Planning a Deck from a Source Document" process in `slide-patterns.md` before writing any HTML: inventory the source, map every item to slides, verify coverage. Every section, decision, data point, specification, and collapsible detail from the source must appear in the deck. If a plan has 7 sections, the deck covers all 7. If there are 6 decisions, present all 6 — not the 2 that fit on one slide. Collapsible details in the source become their own slides. Add more slides rather than cutting content. A 22-slide deck that covers everything beats a 13-slide deck that looks polished but is missing 40% of the source. 327 328 **Slide types (10):** Title, Section Divider, Content, Split, Diagram, Dashboard, Table, Code, Quote, Full-Bleed. Each has a defined layout in `slide-patterns.md`. Content that exceeds a slide's density limit splits across multiple slides — never scrolls within a slide. 329 330 **Visual richness:** Check `which surf` at the start. If surf-cli is available, generate 2–4 images (title slide background, full-bleed background, optional content illustrations) before writing HTML — see the Proactive Imagery section in `slide-patterns.md` for the workflow. Also use SVG decorative accents, per-slide background gradients, inline sparklines, and small Mermaid diagrams. Visual-first, text-second. 331 332 **Compositional variety:** Consecutive slides must vary spatial approach — centered, left-heavy, right-heavy, split, edge-aligned, full-bleed. Three centered slides in a row means push one off-axis. 333 334 **Curated presets:** Four slide-specific presets as starting points (Midnight Editorial, Warm Signal, Terminal Mono, Swiss Clean) plus the existing 8 aesthetic directions adapted for slides. Pick one and commit. See `slide-patterns.md` for preset CSS values. 335 336 **`--slides` flag on existing prompts:** When a user passes `--slides` to `/diff-review`, `/plan-review`, `/project-recap`, or other prompts, the agent gathers data using the prompt's normal data-gathering instructions, then presents the content as a slide deck instead of a scrollable page. The slide version tells the same story with different structure and pacing — but the same breadth of coverage. Don't use the slide format as an excuse to summarize or skip sections that the scrollable version would have included. 337 338 ## File Structure 339 340 Every diagram is a single self-contained `.html` file. No external assets except CDN links (fonts, optional libraries). Structure: 341 342 ```html 343 344 345 346 347 348 Descriptive Title 349 350 353 354 355 356 357 358 359 360 ``` 361 362 ## Sharing Pages 363 364 Share visual explainer pages instantly via Vercel. No account or authentication required. 365 366 **Usage:** 367 ```bash 368 bash {{skill_dir}}/scripts/share.sh 369 ``` 370 371 **Example:** 372 ```bash 373 bash {{skill_dir}}/scripts/share.sh ~/.agent/diagrams/my-diagram.html 374 375 # Output: 376 # ✓ Shared successfully! 377 # Live URL: https://skill-deploy-abc123.vercel.app 378 # Claim URL: https://vercel.com/claim-deployment?code=... 379 ``` 380 381 **How it works:** 382 1. Copies HTML file to temp directory as `index.html` 383 2. Deploys via the vercel-deploy skill (zero-auth claimable deployment) 384 3. URL is live immediately — works in any browser 385 386 **Requirements:** 387 - vercel-deploy skill (should be pre-installed; if not: `pi install npm:vercel-deploy`) 388 389 **Notes:** 390 - Deployments are public — anyone with the URL can view 391 - Preview deployments have configurable retention (default: 30 days) 392 - Claim URL lets you transfer the deployment to your Vercel account 393 394 See `./commands/share.md` for the `/share` command template. 395 396 ## Quality Checks 397 398 Before delivering, verify: 399 - **The squint test**: Blur your eyes. Can you still perceive hierarchy? Are sections visually distinct? 400 - **The swap test**: Would replacing your fonts and colors with a generic dark theme make this indistinguishable from a template? If yes, push the aesthetic further. 401 - **Both themes**: Toggle your OS between light and dark mode. Both should look intentional, not broken. 402 - **Information completeness**: Does the diagram actually convey what the user asked for? Pretty but incomplete is a failure. 403 - **No overflow**: Resize the browser to different widths. No content should clip or escape its container. Every grid and flex child needs `min-width: 0`. Side-by-side panels need `overflow-wrap: break-word`. Never use `display: flex` on `
  • ` for marker characters — it creates anonymous flex items that can't shrink, causing lines with many inline `` badges to overflow. Use absolute positioning for markers instead. See the Overflow Protection section in `./references/css-patterns.md`. 404 - **Mermaid zoom controls**: Every `.mermaid-wrap` container must have zoom controls (+/−/reset/expand buttons), Ctrl/Cmd+scroll zoom, click-and-drag panning, and click-to-expand (clicking without dragging opens the diagram full-size in a new tab). The expand button (⛶) provides the same functionality. See `./references/css-patterns.md` for the full pattern including the `openMermaidInNewTab()` function. 405 - **File opens cleanly**: No console errors, no broken font loads, no layout shifts. 406 407 ## Anti-Patterns (AI Slop) 408 409 These patterns are explicitly forbidden. They signal "AI-generated template" and undermine the skill's purpose of producing distinctive, high-quality diagrams. Review every generated page against this list. 410 411 ### Typography 412 413 **Forbidden fonts as primary `--font-body`:** 414 - Inter — the single most overused AI default 415 - Roboto, Arial, Helvetica — generic system fallbacks promoted to primary 416 - system-ui, sans-serif alone — no character, no intent 417 418 **Required:** Pick from the font pairings in `./references/libraries.md`. Every generation should use a different pairing from the last. 419 420 ### Color Palette 421 422 **Forbidden accent colors:** 423 - Indigo-500/violet-500 (`#8b5cf6`, `#7c3aed`, `#a78bfa`) — Tailwind's default purple range 424 - The cyan + magenta + pink neon gradient combination (`#06b6d4` → `#d946ef` → `#f472b6`) 425 - Any palette that could be described as "Tailwind defaults with purple/pink/cyan accents" 426 427 **Forbidden color effects:** 428 - Gradient text on headings (`background: linear-gradient(...); background-clip: text;`) — this screams AI-generated 429 - Animated glowing box-shadows on cards (`box-shadow: 0 0 20px var(--glow); animation: glow 2s...`) 430 - Multiple overlapping radial glows in accent colors creating a "neon haze" 431 432 **Required:** Build palettes from the reference templates (terracotta/sage, teal/cyan, rose/cranberry, slate/blue) or derive from real IDE themes (Dracula, Nord, Solarized, Gruvbox, Catppuccin). Accents should feel intentional, not default. 433 434 ### Section Headers 435 436 **Forbidden:** 437 - Emoji icons in section headers (🏗️, ⚙️, 📁, 💻, 📅, 🔗, ⚡, 🔧, 📦, 🚀, etc.) 438 - Section headers that all use the same icon-in-rounded-box pattern 439 440 **Required:** Use styled monospace labels with colored dot indicators (see `.section-label` in templates), numbered badges (`section__num` pattern), or asymmetric section dividers. If an icon is genuinely needed, use an inline SVG that matches the palette — not emoji. 441 442 ### Layout & Hierarchy 443 444 **Forbidden:** 445 - Perfectly centered everything with uniform padding 446 - All cards styled identically with the same border-radius, shadow, and spacing 447 - Every section getting equal visual treatment — no hero/primary vs. secondary distinction 448 - Symmetric layouts where left and right halves mirror each other 449 450 **Required:** Vary visual weight. Hero sections should dominate (larger type, more padding, accent-tinted background). Reference sections should feel compact. Use the depth tiers (hero → elevated → default → recessed). Asymmetric layouts create interest. 451 452 ### Template Patterns 453 454 **Forbidden:** 455 - Three-dot window chrome (red/yellow/green dots) on code blocks — this is a cliché 456 - KPI cards where every metric has identical gradient text treatment 457 - "Neon Dashboard" as an aesthetic choice — it always produces generic results 458 - Gradient meshes with pink/purple/cyan blobs in the background 459 460 **Required:** Code blocks use a simple header with filename or language label. KPI cards vary by importance — hero numbers for the primary metric, subdued treatment for supporting metrics. Pick aesthetics with natural constraints: Blueprint (must feel technical/precise), Editorial (must have generous whitespace and serif typography), Paper/ink (must feel warm and informal). 461 462 ### The Slop Test 463 464 Before delivering, apply this test: **Would a developer looking at this page immediately think "AI generated this"?** The telltale signs: 465 466 1. Inter or Roboto font with purple/violet gradient accents 467 2. Every heading has `background-clip: text` gradient 468 3. Emoji icons leading every section 469 4. Glowing cards with animated shadows 470 5. Cyan-magenta-pink color scheme on dark background 471 6. Perfectly uniform card grid with no visual hierarchy 472 7. Three-dot code block chrome 473 474 If two or more of these are present, the page is slop. Regenerate with a different aesthetic direction — Editorial, Blueprint, Paper/ink, or a specific IDE theme. These constrained aesthetics are harder to mess up because they have specific visual requirements that prevent defaulting to generic patterns.

     2	
     3	## Overview
     4	This dataset describes a complete machine learning infrastructure architecture as a directed graph of system components (nodes) and data/control flows (edges). It covers the full ML lifecycle from data ingestion through model serving and operational monitoring, including cross-cutting concerns like data lineage and version control.
     5	
     6	## Data Source
     7	
     8	### ml_architecture
     9	A graph structure with two arrays: `nodes` and `edges`.
    10	
    11	**Nodes** (9 total):
    12	- `id` (string): unique identifier for the component
    13	- `label` (string): display name, may include sub-labels for technology stack
    14	- `layer` (string): architectural layer — one of data, compute, serving, observability, cross-cutting
    15	- `sub_components` (array of strings): specific technologies or sub-systems within the node
    16	- `criticality` (integer, 1–10): operational criticality score
    17	- `category` (string): visual grouping category — data-layer, compute-layer, serving-layer, observability-layer
    18	
    19	**Edges** (15 total):
    20	- `source` / `target` (string): node IDs
    21	- `flow_type` (string): one of primary, feedback, lineage
    22	- `throughput_gbps` (float): data throughput in gigabits per second, range 0.1–12.5
    23	- `label` (string): short description of what flows along the edge
    24	
    25	## Data Notes
    26	- Throughput values are representative estimates for a mid-scale ML platform
    27	- Criticality scores are subjective team assessments
    28	- The graph contains cycles via feedback edges (monitoring → data platform, monitoring → training cluster)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Generate a high-quality ML infrastructure architecture diagram.
Follows visual-explainer skill design principles.
"""

import json
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch, FancyArrowPatch
import numpy as np

# Load data
with open('/app/benchmark/source_data.json') as f:
    data = json.load(f)

nodes = {n['id']: n for n in data['ml_architecture']['nodes']}
edges = data['ml_architecture']['edges']

# Dark theme colors matching skill guidelines
BG_COLOR = '#0f172a'  # deep slate
SURFACE_COLOR = '#1e293b'
TEXT_COLOR = '#e2e8f0'
TEXT_DIM = '#94a3b8'
GRID_COLOR = '#334155'

# Layer colors
LAYER_COLORS = {
    'data-layer': '#3b82f6',      # blue
    'compute-layer': '#22c55e',   # green
    'serving-layer': '#f97316',   # orange
    'observability-layer': '#ef4444',  # red
}

# Layout positions - structured pipeline flow
# Arrange in a grid that shows the pipeline clearly
positions = {
    'data_platform': (1, 6),
    'feature_store': (4, 6),
    'training_cluster': (7, 6),
    'model_registry': (10, 6),
    'inference_online': (13, 7.5),
    'inference_offline': (13, 4.5),
    'ab_experiment': (16, 6),
    'monitoring': (19, 6),
    'version_control': (7, 2.5),
}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(22, 14), facecolor=BG_COLOR)
ax.set_facecolor(BG_COLOR)

# Draw subtle grid
ax.set_xlim(-1, 21)
ax.set_ylim(0, 10)
ax.set_aspect('equal')
ax.axis('off')

# Title
ax.text(10, 9.5, 'ML Infrastructure Architecture Pipeline', 
        fontsize=24, fontweight='bold', color=TEXT_COLOR, ha='center',
        fontfamily='sans-serif')
ax.text(10, 9.0, 'End-to-end data flow from ingestion through monitoring with lineage overlay and feedback loops',
        fontsize=12, color=TEXT_DIM, ha='center', fontfamily='sans-serif')

# Draw edges first (so they appear behind nodes)
for edge in edges:
    src = edge['source']
    tgt = edge['target']
    
    if src not in positions or tgt not in positions:
        continue
    
    x1, y1 = positions[src]
    x2, y2 = positions[tgt]
    
    throughput = edge['throughput_gbps']
    flow_type = edge['flow_type']
    
    # Edge thickness based on throughput
    linewidth = max(0.8, throughput * 1.2)
    
    # Edge style and color
    if flow_type == 'primary':
        color = '#64748b'
        linestyle = '-'
        alpha = 0.7
        zorder = 1
    elif flow_type == 'feedback':
        color = '#f59e0b'  # amber for feedback
        linestyle = '-'
        alpha = 0.8
        zorder = 2
    else:  # lineage
        color = '#a855f7'  # purple for lineage
        linestyle = '--'
        alpha = 0.6
        zorder = 1
    
    # Handle curved edges for feedback and certain lineage
    if flow_type == 'feedback':
        # Curved path for feedback loops
        if src == 'monitoring' and tgt == 'data_platform':
            # Top arc
            connectionstyle = "arc3,rad=0.4"
        elif src == 'monitoring' and tgt == 'training_cluster':
            # Bottom arc
            connectionstyle = "arc3,rad=-0.3"
        else:
            connectionstyle = "arc3,rad=0.1"
        
        arrow = FancyArrowPatch((x1, y1), (x2, y2),
                               arrowstyle='->', mutation_scale=18,
                               linewidth=linewidth, color=color,
                               linestyle=linestyle, alpha=alpha,
                               connectionstyle=connectionstyle,
                               zorder=zorder)
        ax.add_patch(arrow)
    elif flow_type == 'lineage':
        # Curved paths for lineage overlay
        if src == 'version_control' and tgt == 'feature_store':
            connectionstyle = "arc3,rad=0.3"
        elif src == 'version_control' and tgt == 'training_cluster':
            connectionstyle = "arc3,rad=-0.2"
        elif src == 'version_control' and tgt == 'model_registry':
            connectionstyle = "arc3,rad=0.2"
        elif src == 'data_platform' and tgt == 'version_control':
            connectionstyle = "arc3,rad=-0.3"
        else:
            connectionstyle = "arc3,rad=0.1"
        
        arrow = FancyArrowPatch((x1, y1), (x2, y2),
                               arrowstyle='->', mutation_scale=14,
                               linewidth=linewidth, color=color,
                               linestyle=linestyle, alpha=alpha,
                               connectionstyle=connectionstyle,
                               zorder=zorder)
        ax.add_patch(arrow)
    else:
        # Primary flow - straight lines with slight curve for branching
        if src == 'model_registry' and tgt == 'inference_online':
            connectionstyle = "arc3,rad=0.15"
        elif src == 'model_registry' and tgt == 'inference_offline':
            connectionstyle = "arc3,rad=-0.15"
        elif src == 'inference_online' and tgt == 'ab_experiment':
            connectionstyle = "arc3,rad=-0.15"
        elif src == 'inference_offline' and tgt == 'ab_experiment':
            connectionstyle = "arc3,rad=0.15"
        elif src == 'feature_store' and tgt == 'inference_online':
            connectionstyle = "arc3,rad=0.3"
        else:
            connectionstyle = "arc3,rad=0.05"
        
        arrow = FancyArrowPatch((x1, y1), (x2, y2),
                               arrowstyle='->', mutation_scale=16,
                               linewidth=linewidth, color=color,
                               linestyle=linestyle, alpha=alpha,
                               connectionstyle=connectionstyle,
                               zorder=zorder)
        ax.add_patch(arrow)
    
    # Edge label
    mid_x = (x1 + x2) / 2
    mid_y = (y1 + y2) / 2
    
    # Offset labels based on edge type
    if flow_type == 'lineage':
        mid_y -= 0.35
    elif flow_type == 'feedback':
        mid_y += 0.35
    
    ax.text(mid_x, mid_y, f"{edge['label']}\n({throughput} Gbps)",
            fontsize=6.5, color=TEXT_DIM, ha='center', va='center',
            fontfamily='monospace', alpha=0.85,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.15', facecolor=BG_COLOR, 
                     edgecolor='none', alpha=0.85))

# Draw nodes
for node_id, node in nodes.items():
    x, y = positions[node_id]
    category = node['category']
    criticality = node['criticality']
    color = LAYER_COLORS.get(category, '#64748b')
    
    # Node size by criticality
    node_size = 2800 + (criticality * 350)
    
    # Draw node circle
    circle = plt.Circle((x, y), np.sqrt(node_size) / 100, 
                       facecolor=color, edgecolor='white', 
                       linewidth=2.5, alpha=0.9, zorder=5)
    ax.add_patch(circle)
    
    # Inner glow effect
    inner = plt.Circle((x, y), np.sqrt(node_size) / 100 * 0.7,
                      facecolor='white', alpha=0.15, zorder=6)
    ax.add_patch(inner)
    
    # Node label
    label = node['label'].replace('\n', '\n')
    ax.text(x, y + 0.15, label, fontsize=8.5, fontweight='bold',
            color='white', ha='center', va='center',
            fontfamily='sans-serif', zorder=7)
    
    # Criticality badge
    ax.text(x, y - 0.35, f"★ {criticality}", fontsize=7,
            color='white', ha='center', va='center',
            fontfamily='monospace', alpha=0.9, zorder=7)

# Layer legend
legend_x = 0.5
legend_y = 8.5
ax.text(legend_x, legend_y + 0.4, 'Node Layers', fontsize=11, 
        fontweight='bold', color=TEXT_COLOR, fontfamily='sans-serif')

for i, (layer, color) in enumerate(LAYER_COLORS.items()):
    y_pos = legend_y - i * 0.45
    circle = plt.Circle((legend_x, y_pos), 0.12, facecolor=color, 
                       edgecolor='white', linewidth=1, alpha=0.9)
    ax.add_patch(circle)
    ax.text(legend_x + 0.35, y_pos, layer.replace('-', ' ').title(),
            fontsize=9, color=TEXT_COLOR, va='center', fontfamily='sans-serif')

# Edge style legend
edge_legend_x = 0.5
edge_legend_y = 5.8
ax.text(edge_legend_x, edge_legend_y + 0.4, 'Flow Types', fontsize=11,
        fontweight='bold', color=TEXT_COLOR, fontfamily='sans-serif')

edge_styles = [
    ('Primary Data Flow', '#64748b', '-'),
    ('Feedback Loop', '#f59e0b', '-'),
    ('Lineage / Version Control', '#a855f7', '--'),
]

for i, (label, color, style) in enumerate(edge_styles):
    y_pos = edge_legend_y - i * 0.4
    ax.plot([edge_legend_x - 0.15, edge_legend_x + 0.15], [y_pos, y_pos],
            color=color, linewidth=2.5, linestyle=style)
    ax.annotate('', xy=(edge_legend_x + 0.2, y_pos),
                xytext=(edge_legend_x + 0.15, y_pos),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=color, lw=2))
    ax.text(edge_legend_x + 0.4, y_pos, label, fontsize=9,
            color=TEXT_COLOR, va='center', fontfamily='sans-serif')

# Node size legend
size_legend_x = 0.5
size_legend_y = 3.8
ax.text(size_legend_x, size_legend_y + 0.4, 'Criticality', fontsize=11,
        fontweight='bold', color=TEXT_COLOR, fontfamily='sans-serif')

for crit in [7, 8, 9, 10]:
    y_pos = size_legend_y - (crit - 7) * 0.4
    size = 2800 + (crit * 350)
    r = np.sqrt(size) / 100
    circle = plt.Circle((size_legend_x, y_pos), r, facecolor=TEXT_DIM,
                       edgecolor='white', linewidth=1, alpha=0.6)
    ax.add_patch(circle)
    ax.text(size_legend_x + 0.5, y_pos, str(crit), fontsize=8,
            color=TEXT_COLOR, va='center', fontfamily='sans-serif')

# Throughput legend
throughput_legend_x = 0.5
throughput_legend_y = 1.8
ax.text(throughput_legend_x, throughput_legend_y + 0.4, 'Throughput', fontsize=11,
        fontweight='bold', color=TEXT_COLOR, fontfamily='sans-serif')

for t in [0.5, 2.5, 8.0, 12.5]:
    y_pos = throughput_legend_y - (t / 12.5) * 1.2
    lw = max(0.8, t * 1.2)
    ax.plot([throughput_legend_x - 0.2, throughput_legend_x + 0.2], [y_pos, y_pos],
            color=TEXT_DIM, linewidth=lw, alpha=0.7)
    ax.text(throughput_legend_x + 0.4, y_pos, f'{t} Gbps', fontsize=8,
            color=TEXT_COLOR, va='center', fontfamily='sans-serif')

# Add subtle pipeline flow annotation
ax.annotate('Pipeline Flow →', xy=(10, 0.6), fontsize=10, color=TEXT_DIM,
            ha='center', fontfamily='sans-serif', style='italic')

# Feedback loop annotation
ax.annotate('Feedback Loops', xy=(16.5, 8.2), fontsize=9, color='#f59e0b',
            ha='center', fontfamily='sans-serif', style='italic', alpha=0.8)

# Lineage overlay annotation
ax.annotate('Data Lineage & Version Control Overlay', xy=(7, 0.8), fontsize=9,
            color='#a855f7', ha='center', fontfamily='sans-serif', 
            style='italic', alpha=0.8)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('/app/output/result.png', dpi=200, facecolor=BG_COLOR, 
            edgecolor='none', bbox_inches='tight', pad_inches=0.3)
plt.close()

print("Chart saved to /app/output/result.png")

- **Feedback loops** from Monitoring back to Data Platform and Training Cluster
